examples.text: Food travels from the mouth through the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and large intestine before leaving the body as waste.
Food takes a journey: from the mouth down to the stomach, then through the long intestines where nutrients are taken in by the body.

Draw and label: mouth → esophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus. Chewing is mechanical processing; saliva and other secretions help chemical digestion. Nutrients are absorbed mainly in the small intestine. Undigested material leaves through the anus as feces; this elimination differs from kidneys excreting wastes from blood.
The tongue rolls chewed food into a ball and pushes it to the back of the mouth to begin swallowing!

Nutrients are absorbed mainly in the small intestine. Undigested material leaves through the anus as feces; this elimination differs from kidneys excreting wastes from blood.
Digestive organs release juices at the right moments, like saliva when you smell food, so digestion starts on time!

The small intestine is about six meters long, and its folded walls give a huge surface for absorbing nutrients!

Draw a flow chart: digestion breaks food down → nutrients enter blood → circulation delivers them to cells. Cells use nutrients and produce wastes; blood carries many dissolved wastes to the kidneys for excretion in urine. Lungs remove carbon dioxide. These arrows connect digestive, circulatory, excretory and respiratory systems; food itself does not pass through the kidneys.
Excretion removes waste made by your cells, while defecation removes undigested food that never even entered your blood!

If a ring of bark is stripped all the way around a tree trunk, the tree can die because its roots stop getting food.
A plant's stem is like a pipe — it carries water and nutrients from the roots all the way up to the leaves and fruit.
The stem doesn't just hold the plant up — it also carries the food made by the leaves to the rest of the plant!

With the help of surface tension, water climbs up the very thin tubes inside a plant to reach the leaves!

Can a trait skip a generation?

Yes! Sometimes a child has a trait neither parent shows but a grandparent has — this happens when a hidden recessive gene passes quietly through a parent.
A trait that shows up in every generation and appears equally in boys and girls is most likely a dominant trait!

Can a trait skip a generation?

Yes! Sometimes a child has a trait neither parent shows but a grandparent has — this happens when a hidden recessive gene passes quietly through a parent.
In a pedigree chart, a square stands for a male and a circle stands for a female in the family!

What is a Punnett square used for?

It is a grid scientists use to predict the possible traits of offspring, based on the alleles of the parents.

For a hypothetical single-gene trait with complete dominance, cross Aa × Aa. A Punnett square gives AA, Aa, Aa, aa: genotype ratio 1:2:1 and dominant-to-recessive phenotype ratio 3:1. Each offspring has its own probability; four offspring need not match the ratio exactly. Most human traits are more complex than this model.

What does predicting ratios mean?

It means using the parents' genotypes to list possible genotypes and phenotypes of offspring before they are born!

The six-kingdom system sorts all living things into six groups: Archaebacteria, Eubacteria, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, and Animalia!
The five-kingdom system isn't frozen forever — some books now teach six kingdoms since bacteria were split into two groups. Classifying life keeps improving!
The three-domain system groups all life into Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya, based on differences in their cell structures and habitats.

Is Archaea just bacteria?

No! Archaea are their own separate group of life. Like bacteria they lack a nucleus, but scientist Carl Woese used DNA to show their cell chemistry is different.
The six-kingdom system sorts all living things into six groups: Archaebacteria, Eubacteria, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, and Animalia!
The three-domain system groups all life into Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya, based on differences in their cell structures and habitats.
Humans belong to Class Mammalia! Just like other mammals, we have mammary glands that can produce milk to feed our young.
Humans belong to Order Primates, a group of mammals that includes monkeys and apes, because we share grasping hands and forward-facing eyes.
Humans belong to Order Primates, a group of mammals that includes monkeys and apes, because we share grasping hands and forward-facing eyes.
Language, clothes, and cities are just culture! Mammalia and Primates are biological groups based on our body plans.
In the carbon cycle, photosynthesis is when plants absorb gaseous carbon dioxide to build solid glucose molecules!

Draw labelled cycle arrows: air carbon dioxide → plant sugars by photosynthesis → animals by feeding → air carbon dioxide by respiration. Plants respire too. For oxygen, connect photosynthesis releasing oxygen with respiration using it. For water, connect root uptake, leaf transpiration, condensation and rain. Matter cycles; energy flows through and is dispersed as heat.

Rusting is a slow reaction that uses up oxygen from the air, just like burning but much slower!

Most water vapor in the air comes from the oceans because they cover most of Earth's surface!

During photosynthesis, plants take in carbon dioxide from the air to make food.

How does a leaf make food?

Using sunlight, water, and air — a process called photosynthesis!
Plants make their own sugar from sunlight, water, and air in a cool process called photosynthesis!
In the Calvin cycle of photosynthesis, plants use ATP and CO2 to build glucose — the food that powers the plant.
Cellular respiration makes two things as its products: carbon dioxide and water.
The glucose your body uses for respiration comes from the food you eat and digest.
Cellular respiration makes two things as its products: carbon dioxide and water.
Respiration returns carbon dioxide to the air, and plants use that same carbon dioxide again in photosynthesis.
Plant cells have chloroplasts that make food using sunlight!
Chloroplasts are found only in plant cells, and they make food from sunlight through photosynthesis.
Plant cells do two jobs: photosynthesis in the chloroplasts, using sunlight to make food, and cellular respiration in the mitochondria, using that food to release energy.

Consult a reliable biology textbook diagram. In plant cells, photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts. In eukaryotic cells, glycolysis begins in the cytoplasm and most later stages of aerobic respiration occur in mitochondria. Record the reference and label each process separately. Plants carry out respiration as well as photosynthesis.

With your teacher, plan a comparison of plants with and without an available raw material such as carbon dioxide. Keep plant type, light, temperature and duration comparable; include a control and repeated samples. Use teacher-provided starch-test observations as evidence. A surprising result calls for checking the setup, not immediately rejecting the role of the raw material. The teacher handles any chemicals or heating.
We label each setup with its condition, like 'no carbon dioxide' or 'no water,' so we don't mix up the results!

How do we compare the results of our setups?

One setup keeps the raw material as a control, while the other removes it. This way, we can compare the two results!

John Dalton proposed the modern atomic theory, stating that all matter is made of tiny atoms!
Dalton believed the atom was the smallest piece of matter. He thought it could not be divided further!

Who created the 'plum pudding model' of the atom in 1904?

J.J. Thomson created it in 1904.

Who put the nucleus at the center of the atom model?

Ernest Rutherford, in his nuclear model of 1911.

Build a timeline: Dalton’s atomic theory → Thomson’s electron-containing model → Rutherford’s nucleus → Bohr’s energy levels → the quantum model. The current model describes probabilities of finding electrons, not tiny planets on definite paths. Add the evidence that changed each explanation; earlier models remain useful approximations for some tasks.
In the quantum mechanical model, scientists cannot pinpoint an electron's exact location, only the probability of finding it in a region!

Electrons are neatly arranged in special levels or shells all around the center nucleus!
Bohr said electrons travel in fixed paths! They orbit in specific energy levels around the nucleus.
Electrons are neatly arranged in special levels or shells all around the center nucleus!
Bohr said electrons travel in fixed paths! They orbit in specific energy levels around the nucleus.

How do electrons move around the nucleus?

In 1913, Niels Bohr proposed a model where electrons orbit the nucleus just like planets!

How is an atom built in the Bohr model?

It has a tiny center nucleus of protons and neutrons! Electrons orbit around it in fixed energy levels or shells.

Draw a simplified shell diagram for a neutral aluminum-27 atom. Atomic number 13 gives 13 protons and 13 electrons. Mass number 27 gives 27 − 13 = 14 neutrons. Label the nucleus and place electrons in shells as 2, 8, 3. The rings show energy levels, not exact electron paths; do not confuse mass number with average atomic mass.
Protons and neutrons are much heavier than electrons, which are extremely light and tiny!
The proton and neutron are like twins when it comes to weight—they have nearly the same mass!
Here is the neutron! It has absolutely no charge at all, making it perfectly neutral.
Protons and neutrons are much heavier than electrons, which are extremely light and tiny!
Protons and neutrons are much heavier than electrons, which are extremely light and tiny!
The electron is the lightest of the three particles! It is about 1,800 times lighter than a proton. Wow, that's super light!
The proton and neutron are like twins when it comes to weight—they have nearly the same mass!
A proton is a particle with a positive (+) charge found in the atom's center, or nucleus, and it has nearly the same mass as a neutron!

What are the secret symbols for tiny subatomic particles?

A proton's symbol is p+, a neutron is n0, and an electron uses the symbol e-!
A compound like salt always has a fixed, exact amount of the elements joined together!
An element is a pure substance made of only one kind of atom, like oxygen, carbon, or gold!
The atomic number of carbon (C) is 6, so it has exactly 6 protons!
The atomic number of helium (He) is 2, so it has exactly 2 protons!

How did Mendeleev predict undiscovered elements?

He left gaps in his table and correctly predicted elements that had not yet been discovered!

Who created the periodic table of elements back in 1869?

A Russian chemist named Dmitri Mendeleev created this awesome chart to organize all the elements!

How did Mendeleev predict undiscovered elements?

He left gaps in his table and correctly predicted elements that had not yet been discovered!
Moseley used X-rays to show that atomic number, not atomic mass, is the true basis for ordering the elements!
The chemical symbol for oxygen is simply the letter O!
The chemical symbol for hydrogen is simply the letter H!
The chemical symbol for aluminum is Al!
Did you know? The chemical symbol for calcium is Ca!
The chemical symbol for aluminum is Al!
Did you know? The chemical symbol for calcium is Ca!
The noble gases live in Group 18 of the periodic table, and they almost never react with other elements!

Where do halogens live on the periodic table?

The halogens are in Group 17! They are highly reactive nonmetals.
There are 18 groups because electron shells can hold many electrons! Also, transition metals fill inner shells in the middle block.

What do we call the horizontal rows in the periodic table?

They are called periods! The main periodic table has exactly seven periods from left to right.

Where do halogens live on the periodic table?

The halogens are in Group 17! They are highly reactive nonmetals.
The vertical columns in the periodic table are called groups! Elements in the same group share similar properties.
An element's period number tells exactly how many electron shells, or energy levels, its atoms have!
Noble gases like helium, neon, and argon are in Group 18. They almost never react because their outer electron shell is already full!
Noble gases like helium, neon, and argon are in Group 18. They almost never react because their outer electron shell is already full!
The outermost shell of an atom is called the valence shell. Its electrons are the ones that join in chemical bonds!
The atomic number of carbon (C) is 6, so it has exactly 6 protons!
The atomic number of helium (He) is 2, so it has exactly 2 protons!
A boron atom with mass number 11 and atomic number 5 has 5 protons, 5 electrons, and 6 neutrons.
To find the number of neutrons, subtract the atomic number from the mass number! For example, 12 minus 6 gives us 6 neutrons in carbon.

Why do elements in the same group act alike?

Because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell!
Helium has two valence electrons, while other noble gases have eight! This complete set makes them super stable and happy.
Helium has two valence electrons, while other noble gases have eight! This complete set makes them super stable and happy.
Transition metals in the middle columns skip the simple group-number rule for valence electrons, so let's focus on the main groups!
Wow, about 71 percent of Earth's surface is covered by water!
The ocean covers about 71 percent of Earth's surface, which is way more than the land!

How much of Earth is actually dry land?

Only about 29 percent of Earth's surface is land—the rest is water!

How much of Earth is actually land?

Only about 29% of Earth's surface is land! The rest of the surface is water.

How thick is Earth's crust?

The oceanic crust is only about 5 kilometers thick! But the continental crust can be up to 70 kilometers thick.

What rock makes up most of the land beneath our feet?

Granite! It's the main rock of continental crust, made of quartz, feldspar, and mica, with large crystals and a white-to-gray speckled look.

How thick is Earth's crust?

The oceanic crust is only about 5 kilometers thick! But the continental crust can be up to 70 kilometers thick.

What makes a volcano "active"?

An active volcano erupted recently or could erupt again anytime! It is still "alive" inside because hot magma is moving beneath it.

What are the three types of volcanoes?

Volcanoes can be active (able to erupt), dormant (sleeping but able to wake up), or extinct (not expected to ever erupt again)!

Classify volcanoes in separate ways: activity history, eruption style, and tectonic location. Effusive eruptions release flowing lava; explosive eruptions fragment magma or rock. Volcanoes occur at subduction zones, rifts and hotspots. A location or cone shape alone does not tell you whether a volcano is currently active; consult the responsible geological agency.
During the explosive eruption stage of a volcano, high-pressure magma blasts ash and rock fragments high into the atmosphere!

Thin runny lava flows far easily, while thick sticky lava moves slowly and often causes more explosive eruptions!
Runny lava spreads far from the vent before hardening to widen the base, while sticky lava hardens close by to build height!
A stratovolcano is a tall, steep cone built from alternating layers of lava and ash!
Some volcanoes are broad and gently sloped like a shield, while others are steep cones, depending on the kind of lava!
Most active volcanoes form where Earth's huge plates meet! In the Philippines, on the Ring of Fire, one plate sinks under another, melting rock into magma.

Overlay earthquake epicenters, active volcanoes and major mountain belts on a plate map showing oceanic and continental crust. Many clusters follow plate boundaries: subduction zones often have earthquakes and volcanoes; continental collisions build mountains. Exceptions occur within plates, so the pattern is a relationship, not a rule that every event lies exactly on a boundary.

New oceanic crust is born at mid-ocean ridges, while old oceanic crust sinks back into Earth at deep ocean trenches!
The lithosphere is Earth's rigid outer shell made of the crust and the very top of the mantle! It is broken into tectonic plates.

The air inside the eye is warmer than the air around it. This warmth helps keep the typhoon strong!
Warmer oceans give storms more energy, so some typhoons hitting the Philippines can become much stronger!
Warmer oceans give storms more energy, so some typhoons hitting the Philippines can become much stronger!
Typhoons form and gain strength only over warm ocean water, so they weaken quickly after hitting Philippine islands!

Use PAGASA’s tropical-cyclone explanation as a secondary source. Warm ocean water, moist rising air, a developing circulation and suitable winds can support a storm. The Philippines lies in the western North Pacific, a region with frequent tropical cyclones. Record the source and distinguish conditions that favor development from a guarantee that a typhoon will form.
A typhoon tracking record lists the date, time, latitude, and longitude of the storm center for each observation!
Every PAGASA bulletin gives the typhoon's latest coordinates and wind speed, which we use to update the plotted track on our map!
A typhoon tracking record lists the date, time, latitude, and longitude of the storm center for each observation!
Forecasters write observation time in 24-hour format, like 1400, so no one mixes up morning and evening!
The Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) is monitored by PAGASA! If a typhoon enters or forms in the PAR, PAGASA gives it a local name.
Forecasters mark the exact spot where the typhoon crosses the PAR boundary to record when it enters!
A storm surge is higher where the sea is shallow and the coast is flat, because the water piles up easily!
Typhoons form and gain strength only over warm ocean water, so they weaken quickly after hitting Philippine islands!

A typhoon often weakens over land as its circulation is disrupted and its supply of warm, moist ocean air is reduced. Mountains can also force moist air upward, increasing rainfall locally. Landfall does not make a storm harmless: heavy rain, flooding and damaging winds can continue. A mountain range is not a guarantee of protection.
A typhoon weakens after landfall because it loses the warm ocean water that gives it all its energy!

Official warnings come in both Filipino and English so more families can understand and stay safe.

During a full moon, the aligned gravitational pull of the sun and moon creates higher high tides on Philippine beaches!

Does the Sun affect our tides too?

Yes! The Sun affects tides with its gravity, but its pull is weaker than the Moon's.
During a full moon, the aligned gravitational pull of the sun and moon creates higher high tides on Philippine beaches!

When does a spring tide happen?

It's the highest tide! It happens when the Sun, Moon, and Earth line up during a new or full moon.
A neap tide brings the weakest tides! It happens at first quarter and last quarter when the Sun and Moon are at right angles to Earth.
When the Sun and Moon line up at new or full moon, you get the strongest spring tides! At quarter moon, the tides are weaker neap tides.

Use a reliable tidal-energy report to compare sites. A barrage can use the height difference between a basin and the sea to drive turbines as water flows. A useful tidal range is only one factor: engineers also assess cost, habitats, navigation and community needs. Strong tidal currents are another resource, distinct from tidal height difference.
The Bay of Fundy has a huge tidal range! It's a famous world example where the water level changes enough to study for power.
The energy from the rising and falling of ocean tides, called tidal energy, can also be turned into electricity!
The ocean's rise and fall of tides and waves can be turned into electricity! It’s renewable because the ocean keeps moving.

Because g = 9.8 m/s², a falling object speeds up by 9.8 meters per second every second!
Every second you fall on Earth, you speed up by about 9.8 meters per second — that's 9.8 m/s²!
One newton (1 N) is the exact force that gives a 1-kilogram mass an acceleration of 1 m/s²!
Push a heavy cannonball and a light feather with the same force. The feather accelerates much faster because it has much less mass!
A jeepney pulling away from a stop sign speeds up! It is accelerating because its speed is increasing.
Tilted road curves help cars turn safely! The tilt adds extra centripetal force pushing toward the center of the curve.
If you spin a bucket of water fast in a circle, it won't spill! The circular motion keeps pressing the water against the bottom.
In uniform circular motion, an object moves around a circle at a constant speed, but its direction keeps changing at every moment!

For straight motion from rest with uniform acceleration 2 m/s², plot time 0,1,2,3 s against velocity 0,2,4,6 m/s and distance 0,1,4,9 m. Label axes and units: velocity–time is straight, distance–time curves upward. A second velocity record 0,1,4,9 m/s at those times has unequal increases: non-uniform acceleration. Its velocity–time slope changes.
On a distance-time graph, a straight line shows constant speed, but a curve getting steeper means the object is speeding up or accelerating!

Choose east as positive. On a velocity–time graph, plot (0 s, −4 m/s), (1 s, −2 m/s), (2 s, 0 m/s). The straight rising line has constant positive acceleration of 2 m/s², but speed decreases from 4 to 0 m/s. Annotate the axes and direction. Positive acceleration does not always mean speeding up.

What is kinetic energy?

Kinetic energy is the energy of an object that is moving!
The higher an object is above the ground, the more gravitational potential energy it has!
When an object falls down, its stored potential energy changes right into kinetic energy!
At the highest ends of its swing, a pendulum stops for a quick instant before heading back the other way!
At the very top of the highest hill, a roller coaster briefly stops! All its kinetic energy turns into maximum potential energy.
A falling coconut gains kinetic energy as gravity pulls it faster toward the ground!

What does 'work' really mean in science?

Work happens when a force makes an object move some distance!
In physics, no work is done (work = 0) if the object does not move, because Work = Force × Distance and the distance is zero!
If a force pushes at right angles to the direction of motion, it does no work on the object at all!

Does any push or pull count as work?

Work is only done when the force has a part pointing in the direction the object moves!
Power shows how fast work is done! It is calculated by dividing the work by the time taken.

How many joules are in one watt?

One watt equals one joule of energy per second! That means 1 W = 1 joule/second.
The 'watt' measures power, and this cool unit is named after the inventor James Watt!
The watt rating on an appliance like an iron tells you exactly how much energy it uses each second!
Mechanical energy is kinetic plus potential energy still available to do work! This includes lifting, turning, or speeding something up.
Mechanical energy is the total of kinetic energy plus potential energy — without friction, this total stays the same as energy shifts between the two forms!

A lever uses mechanical energy to lift heavy loads! Your push becomes work on the load.

Why do things speed up when falling or rolling downhill?

As an object falls or rolls down, its potential energy turns into kinetic energy, making it go faster!
A roller coaster shows energy conservation: as it drops from a high point, gravitational potential energy turns into kinetic energy — giving it super-fast speed at the bottom!
Every time a ball bounces, it rises a little lower because some energy turns into heat and sound at each hit!

Where does the energy go when a rolling basketball finally stops on the court?

It doesn't just disappear! Its kinetic energy actually transforms into heat and sound instead of vanishing.
In hydropower, falling water from a dam spins the turbine to make clean electricity!
The San Roque Dam in Pangasinan generates electricity by using the kinetic energy of falling water to spin turbines!

In hydroelectric power, fast-flowing water from a dam spins a turbine to generate electricity!
The Angat Dam in Bulacan generates electricity by using the kinetic energy of falling water to spin massive turbines!
The Agus River hydroelectric plant in Iligan City generates electricity by using the kinetic energy of flowing water to spin large turbines!
